open_obligations: Do not transfer compute ratios between the two settings; Hammond and Adam-Day vary verifier width and number of layers, not compute ratio.
Check whether Hammond et al. saw instability with very small verifiers.
Note different protocols (checkability training versus nip).

Note that benefit is measured differently: Hammond and Adam-Day measure verifier capability gained over interacting with a random prover, while Kirchner et al. measure training stability, prover legibility and verifier robustness, and cannot exclude non-optimal hyperparameters as the cause of the poor performance of very small and large verifiers.
in.other_title: Weak verifiers gain most from interacting with a trained prover (nip, graph isomorphism)
in.rationale: Kirchner et al. report checkability training works for verifiers 10^-3 to 10^-1.8 of prover compute, but 10^-4 verifiers make training unstable and prover-sized verifiers do not become robust. Hammond and Adam-Day report on graph isomorphism that verifiers gain capability by interacting with a non-random prover rather than a random one, and that this gain is most pronounced for verifiers which cannot solve the task alone but can after learning to interact with the prover; the settings (checkability training with verifier size as a fraction of prover compute, versus nip on a graph isomorphism task with verifier width and number of layers varied) differ greatly.
in.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: how weak a verifier can be and still benefit from prover-verifier training

state_meaning: AI-drafted candidate; no person has reviewed it.
text: The paper reports that training dynamics are largely unchanged for verifiers from 10^-3 to 10^-1.8 times the prover's compute, but a much smaller verifier (10^-4) makes training unstable and yields weak provers with poor legibility, and a verifier matching the prover's size (10^0) does not become more robust over rounds and yields strong but illegible provers. The authors cannot exclude non-optimal hyperparameters but suggest a too-weak verifier may be unable to verify at all, and a verifier very similar to the prover lets the sneaky prover more easily simulate its mistakes.
title: Checkability training works for mid-range verifier size; fails if too weak or prover-sized
